one_liner: Python generator that emits GPT-2 layers as straight-line C with baked weights; first-party per-layer timings beat PyTorch CPU.
what_it_does: Kaoken reads a Hugging Face GPT-2 checkpoint (dumped to JSON by generate_specification.py) and fills C templates for LayerNorm, GELU, Linear, Conv1D-based attention, MLP and embedding, producing one .c file per layer with the weights written in as numeric literals. Each generated function takes float32_t** input/output buffers of fixed shape; there is no runtime, no model loader and no end-to-end generate() path yet (the README TODO still lists 'get inference working using binary built from c files'). It is a research prototype, not a drop-in replacement for PyTorch or transformers.
how_it_is_fast: Ahead-of-time specialization: shapes and weights are known at generation time, so the generator (utils.unroll_loops plus MAT_MULTIPLY / MAT_MULTIPLY_TRANSPOSE macros) explodes every matrix multiply into one multiply-add expression per output element with constant weights, removing loops, framework dispatch and tensor allocation. LayerNorm uses hand-written ARM NEON intrinsics (vld1q_f32, vaddvq_f32, vdivq_f32). The measured gap also includes PyTorch's per-call Python and dispatch overhead, which dominates at batch 1 and [1,768].
when_to_use: Studying how far constant-folding and full unrolling of a tiny, fixed-shape layer can go on an ARM64 (Apple Silicon) CPU with clang -O3.
Prototyping a code-generation backend for a very small model whose weights fit comfortably in generated source.
As a teaching example of turning a PyTorch module into specialized C, with the PyTorch validation scripts as reference outputs.
when_not_to_use: Real GPT-2 or any real model inference: the README says baked attention with actual GPT-2 weights (16k lines of C) could not be compiled on a MacBook Air, and no end-to-end model.generate() benchmark exists.
x86-64 or any non-ARM target: the templates include arm_neon.h and the Makefile hard-codes clang -arch arm64.
Large layers such as the lm_head Linear [768 x 50257]: fully unrolled, that is about 38.6 million literal multiply-adds in one function, so compile time, memory and code size are prohibitive.
Models whose weights change or need quantization; every weight change means regenerating and recompiling the C.
Anything that needs a maintained project: 17 commits over about one month in late 2024, no releases, no tests beyond the validation scripts.

integration.dependencies: Generation: Python with torch 2.0.1, transformers 4.34.1, numpy 1.26.1 (requirements.txt) and a local GPT-2 checkout; generated code: libc and libm only
integration.min_toolchain: clang with ARM NEON support (Makefile: clang -arch arm64 -O3); C standard not documented
integration.platforms: aarch64 only (arm_neon.h, -arch arm64); Apple Silicon implied by the Makefile and the README's MacBook Air mention
integration.thread_safety: not documented; generated attention code keeps intermediate results in global heap buffers (gpt2_attention_0_c_attn_temp etc.), so concurrent calls into the same layer would race

gotchas: The committed generated/*.c files are toy shapes (10x10 Linear, 4-element LayerNorm, embedding size 8 attention), not the [1,768] and [768,50257] shapes in the benchmark table; the code that produced the table is not in the repo.

The validation Linear weights repeat the same row for every output feature (every row is 0.1*(i+1)), and the committed 10x10 test bakes 0.1 everywhere, so after unrolling every output is the same expression and clang -O3 can fold them into a single dot product; the 22.4 ms vs 2.378 ms Linear ratio may not reflect real lm_head work.
Weights are baked as double literals (e.g. input[0][1] * 0.1) and GELU calls pow/tanh/sqrt in double with pi approximated as 3.14159, so results drift slightly from PyTorch's float32 math.pi version.
Generated code mallocs its buffers and never frees them, and attention needs gpt2_attention_0_initialize_heap_memory() called first.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Kaoken only to study baked-weight code generation on ARM; CodeJeNN is the closer working 'emit C++ from a trained model' tool, llm.c's train_gpt2.c is a readable, working plain-C GPT-2, and CTranslate2 or OpenVINO are what to deploy for real CPU transformer inference.
verified_claims_summary: The README table times single PyTorch layer calls (time.time(), no warm-up) against single generated-C calls (clock()), averaged over five runs, on an unstated ARM64 machine (MacBook Air implied) with torch 2.0.1 pinned: LayerNorm [1,768] 0.052 vs 0.0052 ms, GELU 0.174 vs 0.084 ms, Linear [768,50257] 22.4 vs 2.378 ms, Attention 14.484 vs 9.386 ms, all with synthetic patterned weights rather than GPT-2's. The margin likely comes mostly from PyTorch cold-call overhead and constant folding over repeated weights.
status_note: Stale prototype (last commit 2024-11-16, 17 commits, 4 stars), MIT-licensed so code is copyable, but nothing works end to end and it needs regeneration per model.
